patients.label: 56-year-old postmenopausal woman with anaphylactic shock after intravenous ondansetron

identity_evidence.quote: The patient, a 56-year-old female with no known comorbidities
A 56-year-old postmenopausal woman presented to the Emergency Department

attribution_limitations: The test is called a skin prick test in the title, abstract-level wording and case text, but the Figure 1 caption calls panel A the "intradermal injection site".

The case text reports the serum tryptase of 45 µg/L in "Further blood tests" without a time, while the Table 1 caption labels every table value, including serum tryptase, as a finding on admission at presentation. The table cell and the text statement are kept as separate facts.

The abstract lists Ringer's Lactate fluids as administered together with ondansetron, whereas the case text introduces Ringer’s Lactate as part of the resuscitation after the reaction. The source does not say whether these are one or two fluid administrations.
The 5 minute wheal of about 10 mm and the 30 minute wheal of about 20 mm come only from the Figure 1 caption; the case text gives a 20 mm wheal without a time.
The abstract says the nausea and vomiting were "possibly due to" unhygienic, undercooked food; gastroenteritis appears only as the Table 2 Primary Disease/Indication cell for this case.
The discussion sentence that limited response to intramuscular adrenaline may have been due to reduced absorption during shock is an explanation offered by the authors, not a documented finding.

evidence.quote: (A) At 0 minutes: baseline appearance at the intradermal injection site.
(B) At 5 minutes: development of a visible wheal (~10 mm) with surrounding flare, although the erythema is subtle in the photograph.
(C) At 30 minutes: persistent erythematous wheal (~20 mm), confirming hypersensitivity.

limitations: Table 2 rows other than "Our case" and the discussion of cited published cases (82-year-old woman, 70-year-old man) describe other patients or literature and are not recorded as facts about the index patient.

Intro and discussion statements about ondansetron safety, incidence, mechanisms and recommendations (for example slow intravenous administration) are general and are not recorded as patient facts or care plans.
The vasopressor drug, dose and route are not named; the drug used for rapid sequence induction is not named.

Dates, the interval between presentation and the later tests, and the time of the text tryptase draw are not stated; whether "on admission" for Table 1 means emergency or ICU admission is not stated; no order beyond the stated relations was added.
Figure 1 was inspected in the separate visual target; caption-layer visual status here remains not_inspected.

claims.text: A 56-year-old postmenopausal woman with no known comorbidities presented to the Emergency Department with diarrhea for five days and persistent vomiting for one day after eating undercooked street food. She was conscious, afebrile and hemodynamically stable with a pulse of 110/minute, blood pressure 130/80 mmHg and SpO2 98% on room air, and had signs of dehydration. Admission laboratory values in Table 1 were within normal limits except serum tryptase.
